blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Gujarat's ancient past stretches from the Indus Valley Civilization to early historical kingdoms.
The Chaulukya (Solanki) era from 942 to 1244 CE is considered a high point in Gujarat's medieval history.
The Gujarat Sultanate maintained independent governance from 1407 until its conquest by Akbar in 1572 CE.
Mughal authority established administrative control over Gujarat from 1572 to 1758 CE before Maratha dominance.
Modern Gujarat's political identity developed through the Indian freedom movement, leading to its formation as an independent state.

blocks.content: Gujarat has one of the richest ancient histories in India. The region was home to one of the world's oldest civilizations — the Indus Valley Civilization (Harappan Civilization), which flourished around 2500 BCE.
1.1.1 Indus Valley Civilization Sites in Gujarat
Gujarat is exceptionally rich in Harappan sites, with major excavations providing invaluable evidence of Bronze Age civilization in the region.

items: Lothal (Ahmedabad District): One of the most important ancient cities. Contains the world's oldest known dockyard (around 2400 BCE). Excavated by S.R. Rao in 1954-63. Evidence of bead-making, copper tools, and trade with Mesopotamia.

Dholavira (Kutch District): A UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed 2021). One of the five largest Harappan sites. Known for its water conservation systems, large stadium-like structure, and a signboard with Harappan script.
Rangpur (Surendranagar District): Shows transition from Harappan to post-Harappan culture.
Rojdi (Rajkot District): Important Harappan-era site with evidence of cattle rearing and agriculture.
Surkotada (Kutch District): Famous for the discovery of horse remains, one of the earliest proofs of horse use in ancient India.
Kuntasi (Morbi District): Coastal Harappan site showing evidence of maritime trade.

blocks.content: After the Harappan decline, various tribes and kingdoms rose to prominence in the Gujarat region.

items: The Mauryan Empire under Chandragupta Maurya extended into Gujarat. Ashoka's rock edicts are found at Junagadh (Girnar), Sopara, and other places, proving Mauryan presence in the region.

The Kshatrapas (Satraps): Western Kshatrapas ruled much of Gujarat from 1st century CE to 4th century CE. Their capital was Ujjain. They were eventually defeated by Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) of the Gupta dynasty.
Gupta Period: Gujarat was part of the Gupta Empire from the 4th to 6th century CE. The Gupta era saw flourishing trade, art, and architecture in the region.

blocks.content: The Maitrakas, originally Gupta governors, declared independence after the decline of the Gupta Empire and established their kingdom with capital at Valabhi (present-day Vala near Bhavnagar). Valabhi became a major center of Buddhist learning and trade. The famous Valabhi University attracted scholars from across Asia.
The Solanki dynasty is considered the Golden Age of Gujarat. They ruled from Anhilwara (present-day Patan in North Gujarat).

items: Mularaja I (942–995 CE): Founded the Solanki/Chaulukya dynasty. Built the Rudra Mahalaya temple at Sidhpur.
Bhimdev I (1022–1064 CE): Famous for his conflicts with Mahmud of Ghazni who attacked Somnath in 1025 CE.
Kumarpal (1143–1172 CE): A devout Jain king who outlawed animal slaughter. The Jain philosopher Hemachandra was his mentor.
Siddharaj Jayasinh (1094–1143 CE): Greatest Solanki ruler. Built the Sahasralinga Lake at Patan. Patron of art and literature. Capital Anhilwara reached its peak under him.

blocks.content: After the Solanki decline, the Vaghelas, originally ministers of the Solankis, took power. The last Vaghela ruler, Karna II (Karnadeva II), was defeated by Alauddin Khilji's forces in 1297 CE, bringing Gujarat under the Delhi Sultanate.

Gujarat was under the Delhi Sultanate from 1297 CE. Various governors were appointed from Delhi. Zafar Khan (later Sultan Ahmad Shah) revolted and established independent Gujarat Sultanate in 1407 CE.
The Gujarat Sultanate was a powerful independent kingdom that reached the peak of its glory under several capable rulers.

items: Ahmad Shah I (1411–1442 CE): Founded Ahmedabad in 1411 CE. Named after the three Ahmed saints buried there (Ahmad Shah, Qazi Ahmed, Malik Ahmed). Built Teen Darwaza, Jama Masjid.

Muhammad Shah II (Begada) (1458–1511 CE): Most powerful Gujarat sultan. Conquered Junagadh (1469) and Champaner (1484). Built Champaner-Pavagadh complex (UNESCO World Heritage Site). Had fierce conflicts with the Portuguese.
Mahmud Shah II: Last independent sultan. Gujarat was annexed by Akbar in 1572 CE.

blocks.content: Emperor Akbar personally led the campaign to annex Gujarat in 1572 CE. He appointed governors (Subedars) to administer the region. Todar Mal, Akbar's revenue minister, conducted land surveys in Gujarat. Under Aurangzeb, Gujarat faced religious tensions and political instability.

items: Idar: A Rajput princely state in Gujarat that maintained relative autonomy during Mughal rule.
Surat: Became the most important port city during Mughal times. The Surat factories of European powers — Portuguese, Dutch, English, and French — operated from here.

blocks.content: After Aurangzeb's death, Maratha power expanded into Gujarat. The Peshwas, Gaekwads of Baroda, and Scindias all had influence in various parts of Gujarat. The Gaekwad dynasty of Baroda (Vadodara) became the most prominent Maratha power in Gujarat, eventually becoming a princely state under British paramountcy.

The British East India Company established its first factory in India at Surat in 1608 CE. Captain Thomas Best defeated Portuguese naval forces in 1612, strengthening British presence. By the 19th century, British power was dominant across Gujarat through various treaties and annexations.
During British rule, Gujarat had numerous princely states. Some prominent ones were:

cells: Gaekwad dynasty; Sayajirao III was a reformer

items: Pay close attention to the chronological succession: Maitrakas (470–788 CE) → Chaulukyas (942–1244 CE) → Vaghelas (1244–1304 CE).
Key year to remember: 1572 CE marks the beginning of Mughal Rule in Gujarat under Emperor Akbar.
Distinguish between the independent Gujarat Sultanate (1407–1572 CE) and the subsequent Mughal integration period.

blocks.content: Gujarat played a pivotal role in India's independence movement, largely due to the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.

items: Champaran Satyagraha (1917): Gandhi's first Satyagraha in India, though in Bihar, it marked his formal entry into Indian politics.
Kheda Satyagraha (1918): Gandhi led peasants of Kheda district to protest against the British demand for full land revenue despite crop failure. This was the first successful Satyagraha in Gujarat.
Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918): Gandhi conducted a hunger strike to support mill workers demanding a 35% wage increase. Workers eventually got 35% hike.
Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22): Gujarat saw massive participation. Courts boycotted, foreign cloth burned, schools abandoned.

Bardoli Satyagraha (1928): Led by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, farmers of Bardoli taluka refused to pay increased land revenue. The government was forced to withdraw the hike. Patel earned the title 'Sardar' here.

Salt Satyagraha / Dandi March (1930): Gandhi walked 241 miles from Sabarmati Ashram, Ahmedabad to Dandi village in Navsari district to make salt, defying British salt laws. This was a landmark event in the independence movement.
Quit India Movement (1942): Gujarat saw widespread participation. Many leaders were arrested including Patel and other Congress leaders.

blocks.content: After Independence, the former British provinces and princely states were reorganized. Gujarat was part of the Bombay State initially. Following the States Reorganisation Act 1956, the Bombay State was enlarged. The Mahagujarat Movement (1956–1960) demanded a separate Gujarati-speaking state.

items: Mahagujarat Movement: Led by Indulal Yagnik and others. Major protests took place, particularly after the Mumbai Police fired on protesters on November 1, 1956 (known as the Black Day).
Formation of Gujarat: On May 1, 1960, the Bombay Reorganisation Act came into effect, and Gujarat became a separate state. May 1 is celebrated as Gujarat Foundation Day (Sthapna Divas).
First Chief Minister: Dr. Jivraj Narayan Mehta (1960–1963).
First Governor: Mehdi Nawaz Jung.
Capital: Ahmedabad was the provisional capital; Gandhinagar became the permanent capital in 1971.
